::: {.oneline}
A Green function is the amplitude for putting a particle into the system at one
place and time and finding it at another, with everything else in the system
free to react while it travels.
:::

## Short answer

Suppose we drop an extra electron into a metal and ask what happens next. It
moves, but it also pushes the other electrons out of its way, and they push
back. What travels onwards is therefore not the bare electron we injected, but
the electron together with the disturbance it drags along.

The Green function is the amplitude for this whole process, that is, inject
here and look there later. It answers two questions at once: where the particle
can go, and for how long it remains recognizable as a particle before its energy
is shared out among everything else.

Read in terms of energy rather than time, the same object shows sharp features
at the energies for which an added particle is long lived, and broad features
where it decays quickly. These are the quasiparticles, which are not the
original electrons but the composite objects that actually propagate. A band
structure is thus what the sharp features look like when the system is
well-behaved enough for them to be sharp.

This is also the point at which the single-particle picture is derived rather
than assumed. Bands are not a starting assumption about materials, but what the
Green function looks like in a regime where a dressed electron survives long
enough to be called a particle.

## Why it works this way

Interacting systems have far too many states to describe individually, but most
experiments do not need them. Photoemission removes an electron and tunnelling
adds one, so that both ask what happens when the particle number changes by one.
The Green function is precisely the answer to that question, with everything
else summarized rather than enumerated.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## The algebra: definition and poles

The time-ordered single-particle Green function is

$$
G(\mathbf r t, \mathbf r' t') = -\frac{i}{\hbar}
\big\langle \mathcal{T}\, \hat\psi(\mathbf r t)\,
\hat\psi^\dagger(\mathbf r' t') \big\rangle .
$$ {#eq-green-definition}

Its Lehmann representation shows poles at the exact energies for adding or
removing one particle, weighted by the overlap of the resulting state with a
single-particle excitation:

$$
G(\omega) = \sum_n \frac{|\langle n \rvert \hat\psi^\dagger \lvert 0\rangle|^2}
{\omega - (E_n - E_0) + i\eta} + \dots
$$ {#eq-lehmann}

The spectral function $A(\omega) = -\frac{1}{\pi}\operatorname{Im} G(\omega)$ is
what photoemission measures, up to matrix elements and geometry.
:::

## Common confusions

- **"The Green function describes an electron."** It describes an electron
  together with the rearrangement it causes, and in a strongly correlated system
  these can be very different objects.
- **"Its poles are the excitation energies of the system."** They are *charged*
  excitation energies, obtained by adding or removing a particle. Neutral
  excitations such as excitons live in the
  [response function](../what-is-a-response-function/index.qmd) instead.
